chunks.label: 1-EASY
chunks.text:
Demand not that events should happen as you wish; but wish them to happen
as they do happen, and you will go on well.

chunks.label: 2-LONG
chunks.text:
In my father, I observed his meekness; his constancy without
wavering in those things, which after a due examination and
deliberation, he had determined. How free from all vanity he carried
himself in matter of honour. His industry and assiduity, his readiness
to hear any man, that had aught to say tending to any common good:
how generally and impartially he would give every man his due. His
skill and knowledge, when rigour or extremity, or when remissness
or moderation was in season. How he did abstain from all unchaste
love of youths. His moderate condescension to other men's occasions
as an ordinary man, neither absolutely requiring of his friends, that
they should wait upon him at his ordinary meals, nor that they should
necessitate of themselves to go along with him in his journeys;
and that whensoever any had been left behind upon any occasion,
they ever found him the same towards them. His accurate and moderate
consideration in all things upon due deliberation, without any
hurry at all. His constancy and uniformity in his friendships.
His toleration of them that were truly bold and open: and the pleasure
that he took in them that could tell him of a better course, without
any offence. His religion without superstition. All these things
in him, were without affectation and ostentation. Besides all these
things in him, this is also to be observed, that he of all men was
least subject to be wearied. His singular ability both to endure
labour, and to continue constant and uniform in both. I remember
also, that he had a trick of countenance and fashion, that after
he had attentively heard any man he ever left off with the same
countenance showing neither dislike nor approbation. His care of
the body; which was such, that he that regarded it might well
perceive, that he did not much fancy living; but however, not as
naturally neglecting it, by his great temperance and moderation
in meat and drink, in his exercises, and in the use of other things
about him, he had brought himself to such a habit of body that he
was neither too fat nor too lean. How void of pride and ostentation
he was, and how easily contented with few things; as lodging, and
bedding, and apparel, and servants, and diet, and attendance. How
hard he applied himself, and how patiently. A man, how to his great
frugality, able to hold out and to endure till the evening,
not so much as needing to be refreshed by any other passage of
refection, besides his ordinary meal. His constancy and equality in
friendship. His bearing with those that openly and with all liberty
opposed his opinions; and even rejoicing if any man could better
advise him: and lastly, his religion without superstition. All
these things in him I must remember: that when mine hour is come, my
conscience may be as clear and ready as his.

chunks.label: 3-ARCHAIC
chunks.description: Dense archaic language with thou/thee (Enchiridion section 51)
chunks.text:
The first and most necessary topic in philosophy is the practical
application of principles, as, _We ought not to lie_; the second is that
of demonstrations as, _Why it is that we ought not to lie_; the third,
that which gives strength and logical connection to the other two, as,
_Why this is a demonstration_. For what is demonstration? What is a
consequence? What a contradiction? What truth? What falsehood? The third
topic, then, is necessary on account of the second; and the second on
account of the first. But the most necessary, and that whereon we ought
to rest, is the first. But we do just the contrary. For we spend all our
time on the third topic, and employ all our diligence about that, and
entirely neglect the first. Therefore, at the same time that we lie, we
are very ready to show how it is demonstrated that lying is wrong.

chunks.label: 4-SENECA
chunks.description: Conversational Seneca tone (Shortness of Life section 1)
chunks.text: The greater part of mankind, my Paulinus, complains of the unkindness of Nature, because we are born only for a short space of time, and that this allotted period of life runs away so swiftly, nay, so hurriedly, that with very few exceptions men's life comes to an end just as they are preparing to enjoy it: nor is it only the common people and the ignorant vulgar who mourn over this universal misfortune, as they consider it: this feeling has wrung complaints even from the greatest men.

chunks.label: 5-FRAGMENT
chunks.description: Very short fragment, 1-2 sentences (Meditations Book 4, section 2)
chunks.text:
Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according
to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
